prompt: Choosing a disk for a busy PostgreSQL server, a colleague points at an NVMe drive rated at 7 000 MB/s. Why does that figure not tell you how many commits a second the server will sustain?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 1; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 9.

choices.text: It is the speed of the connection to the board, and the chips behind it are slower still
choices.why: That confuses the connection with the drive; NVMe and SATA name how a drive is connected, and neither figure counts flushes.

choices.text: It holds for commits as well, as long as about a tenth of the drive is kept free
choices.why: Free space is the one place capacity touches speed, and it does not turn throughput into commits.

choices.text: It counts large transfers; a commit waits on a small flush, which `pg_test_fsync` measures
choices.why: Right: throughput and flushes per second are different questions, and a busy server waits on the second.

choices.text: It is a reading figure, and the box gives writing as a second MB/s figure
choices.why: A write figure in MB/s is still throughput; a commit's flush is a few kilobytes, and it is counted per second.

prompt: `pg_test_fsync` on a new server reports well over a million `fdatasync` flushes a second. Its disk answers from a write cache with no battery behind it, keeping its promise in ___ memory that a power cut erases, committed transactions included.
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 1; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 9.

prompt: A 4 GB server runs PostgreSQL with `work_mem` raised to 64MB for everybody. On Monday morning twenty people open the same dashboard report, and the whole machine crawls: the disk is busy and the processor mostly idle. What is going on?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 1; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 6.

choices.text: Their sorts and hashes outgrew memory, so the system is moving memory out to disk
choices.why: Right: each step may take `work_mem` and twenty reports multiply it, and a full memory swaps.

choices.text: `shared_buffers` is too small, so every page has to come from the disk
choices.why: Giving the cache more would take memory from a machine already out of it; the symptom is memory, not cache misses.

choices.text: Twenty reports are more than the processor can handle, and the idle figure is lagging
choices.why: An idle processor is the evidence, not a misreading: the work is waiting on the disk.

choices.text: `work_mem` caps each connection at 64MB, so the reports spill to temporary files
choices.why: `work_mem` is a ceiling per sort or hash, not per connection, and nothing adds the steps up.

prompt: The shop's nightly dump of its database is written to a USB drive that stays plugged into the database server. Why will that copy not survive a ransomware attack on the server?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 8; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 10.

choices.text: It would survive if each dump file were encrypted with a password of its own
choices.why: Encryption keeps the contents from being read; the intruder can still delete or encrypt the file over it.

choices.text: It would survive if every dump were restored the next morning to prove it works
choices.why: A restore proves the copy is good; it does nothing to stop the intruder reaching it.

choices.text: It would survive if the drive kept a week of dumps rather than only last night's
choices.why: Every one of those dumps sits on the same connected drive, so all of them are reached together.

choices.text: Always attached, it is one more folder for whoever takes that machine
choices.why: Right: an attacker goes for the backups first, and a drive that is always connected is part of the machine.

prompt: A developer argues the shop needs no backups, because a standby receives every change the primary makes within a second. What is the flaw in that argument?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 11; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 11.

choices.text: A standby counts as a copy only when its disk is a different model
choices.why: That borrows the rule about two kinds of media, and a different disk would still receive the same change.

choices.text: A copy built to change when the original does also receives a mistaken `DELETE`
choices.why: Right: like sync, replication copies the mistake, and a backup is a copy that does not change.

choices.text: A second is too slow; only a standby that confirms each commit before it returns can stand in
choices.why: Speed makes it worse, not better: the faster the copy, the sooner the mistake arrives.

choices.text: A standby sits on another machine, so it cannot be restored from directly
choices.why: Being elsewhere is what an offsite backup wants; the trouble is that it follows every change.

prompt: A processor needs a piece of data. Put the places it can find it in order, nearest and fastest first.
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 1.
items: registers
cache
memory (RAM)
an SSD
a hard disk
trap: Putting cache after memory, as if it were extra RAM; it lives inside the processor and is reached in about 5 ns.

prompt: Each event below loses a database's data. Match it to the way of losing data it belongs to, among the four the computing course names.
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 8; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 11.

pairs.right: you delete it
the hardware fails

pairs.left: a flood in the server room
pairs.right: the machine goes
something changes the files while you still have them

prompt: The shop's application suddenly cannot reach its database. The chain runs through the application's settings, the name lookup, the network, the firewall and the database server. By the lesson's method, what is the best first test?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 14.

choices.text: Restart the database server first, as it is the likeliest cause
choices.why: Fixing the likeliest cause first has no structure: three wrong guesses leave you where you began.

choices.text: Check the settings, then the name, then the network, until one fails
choices.why: Link by link, a test that passes tells you almost nothing; halving rules out half either way.

choices.text: Change the firewall rule and the settings together, then try again
choices.why: Two changes at once leave you unable to say which one mattered.

choices.text: Try a known-good client from the application's machine, a cheap cut
choices.why: Right: it splits the application's own settings from everything after them, and it costs a minute.

prompt: A report needs 1 000 pages scattered across a hard disk, none of them in memory, and each has to be reached separately. Using the lesson's figure for reaching one thing on a hard disk, about how many seconds does the reaching alone take?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 1.

prompt: The shop's application finds its primary database through `db.shop.example`, whose record has a TTL of 86400. On Saturday the team will move the primary to another server by changing that record. What should happen first, and when?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 19.

choices.text: Lower the TTL to about sixty seconds at least a day ahead, as that change waits out the old TTL
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Change the record on Saturday, then lower the TTL so the new address spreads faster
choices.why: Lowering it afterwards changes nothing for the copies already cached under the old TTL.

choices.text: Change the record on Saturday and allow forty-eight hours for it to propagate
choices.why: Nothing propagates; the longest wait is one TTL, and forty-eight hours belongs to changing nameservers.

choices.text: Move the domain to a DNS provider whose servers push each change out at once
choices.why: No server pushes anything to resolvers, and changing nameservers is the slow kind of change.

prompt: A page lists fifty customers and loads each one's orders lazily: one query for the list, then one per customer. The application stays in São Paulo and the database moves to Miami. At the round-trip floor the lesson gives for that route, at least how many milliseconds does the page spend crossing to the database?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 3; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 11.

prompt: A standby opens a connection to the primary and receives the write-ahead log as it is written. In that exchange, which machine plays the client?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 1; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 11.

choices.text: The primary, since it is the one sending the data across
choices.why: Sending most of the bytes is not the role; the client is whoever starts the exchange and asks.

choices.text: The standby, because it opens the connection and asks for the log
choices.why: Right: the role belongs to the exchange, so a database server can be a client too.

choices.text: Neither: two database servers talking to each other is peer-to-peer
choices.why: Each connection still has one side that asks and one that answers; two servers do not change that.

choices.text: The standby, because it is the smaller and less important machine
choices.why: Size and importance do not decide the role; a small machine that answers is a server.

prompt: The shop moves its PostgreSQL from its own VPS to a provider's managed database. Which jobs are still the shop's afterwards? Choose all that apply.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 9; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 3.

choices.text: Taking the nightly backups of the data
choices.why: A managed database is the case where somebody else takes the backups.

choices.text: Deciding the roles and what each one may read
choices.why: Right: roles and grants live inside the database, wherever the server is.

choices.text: Choosing when to move to the next major version
choices.why: Right: the console only carries out that decision; it does not make it.

choices.text: Applying the minor-version updates to the server
choices.why: The provider applies minor versions; the decision left to the shop is the major one.

prompt: A colleague in another office types the database container's address, `172.17.0.2`, into a client, and nothing answers. Addresses in the `172.16`–`172.31` range are ___, so nothing on the internet routes to them.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 4; Docker and Containers, lesson 23.

prompt: During the nightly report, the proxy in front of the shop's application logs `504 Gateway Timeout` for some requests. What does that code say happened?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: The application answered, but with something the proxy could not read
choices.why: That is `502`: the thing behind the proxy answered badly.

choices.text: The application is up and refusing on purpose, for maintenance
choices.why: That is `503`, a service deliberately not serving.

choices.text: The application behind the proxy never answered in time
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The browser sent a request that the proxy could not make sense of
choices.why: That would be a `4xx`, the client's fault; a `5xx` points at the server side.

prompt: A staff laptop is stolen while signed in to the shop's admin pages. Sessions are rows in a table on the server, and the cookie holds only an identifier. What ends that laptop's session at once?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: Deleting that row from the server's table
choices.why: Right: the identifier then points at nothing, and that is ending the session from your side.

choices.text: Changing the staff member's password, which the cookie carries
choices.why: The cookie carries an identifier and nothing else; the password was never in it.

choices.text: Waiting for the idle timeout, which ends it after a quiet period
choices.why: That ends it eventually, and only if the thief stays quiet; it is not at once.

choices.text: Sending a response that tells that browser to drop its cookie
choices.why: A response only reaches the laptop if it asks for something, and the thief chooses that.

prompt: So that the monitoring account can read file sizes, a colleague runs `sudo chmod -R 755 /var/lib/postgresql/16/main`. What happens at the next restart of PostgreSQL?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 4.

choices.text: It starts, and every account can now list `base/` and read the sizes
choices.why: That is what the mode allows on Linux; the server checks its directory before it lets that stand.

choices.text: It starts, but the files are now executable and the server reads none
choices.why: An execute bit on a data file changes nothing for the server; the open directory is the problem.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the postgres account's umask still applies
choices.why: A umask acts only when a file is created; `chmod` is absolute.

choices.text: The server refuses to start, as its directory is open to other accounts
choices.why: Right: the sizes are asked of the server, with its size functions.

prompt: On an Ubuntu database server, `systemctl status postgresql` reports `active (exited)`, while `psql` answers `No such file or directory` and asks whether the server is running. What do you look at next?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 3.

choices.text: Nothing on the server: `active (exited)` means the job ran and is healthy
choices.why: That unit only passes commands to the clusters; its success says nothing about the postmaster.

choices.text: The cluster's own unit, `systemctl status postgresql@16-main`
choices.why: Right: that unit holds the postmaster, and its status and journal say why it is down.

choices.text: `systemctl enable postgresql`, since `exited` means it will not start at boot
choices.why: Whether a unit starts at boot is the `Loaded:` line, not the `Active:` one.

choices.text: `systemctl restart postgresql`, because `exited` is how a crash is shown
choices.why: A unit that stopped and should not have reads `failed`; restarting before reading loses the reason.

prompt: A reporting service connects to a database on another machine as it starts. After every reboot it fails once, and `systemctl start` by hand always works. Its unit says `After=network.target`. What does the lesson change?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

choices.text: `Requires=network.target`, so the service fails along with the network
choices.why: That adds a dependency; `network.target` is still reached before the network can carry anything.

choices.text: `After=postgresql.service`, so the database is started before the report
choices.why: The database is on another machine; a local unit's order says nothing about it.

choices.text: `After=` and `Wants=network-online.target`, with the wait-online service enabled
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `Type=forking`, so systemd waits for the service to finish starting
choices.why: `forking` is for a program that daemonises itself; on one that does not, the start hangs.

prompt: After a reboot, the database does not answer and you suspect its service. Put the checks in the order the lesson runs them.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 3.
items: `systemctl --failed`, to see which units failed
`systemctl status postgresql@16-main`, read in order
`journalctl -u postgresql@16-main -n 50`, for more of its log
`journalctl -b -p err`, for a cause elsewhere on the machine
trap: Opening the whole boot's errors first buries the cluster's own message, which its status block usually shows on the first screen.

prompt: A runaway session holds locks, and `ps` shows its backend as pid 4821. A colleague is about to type `sudo kill -9 4821`. What do you tell them?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 10.

choices.text: Go ahead: `KILL` cannot be ignored, and only that session ends
choices.why: The postmaster treats a killed backend as a crash and restarts every process.

choices.text: `kill -HUP 4821` instead, so the backend rereads its settings and lets go
choices.why: `HUP` asks for the configuration to be read again; the transaction and its locks stay.

choices.text: `sudo kill 4821` instead, which ends just that one session, cleanly
choices.why: Right: `TERM` is what `pg_terminate_backend` sends.

choices.text: Send `-9` to the postmaster instead, so that its children stop with it
choices.why: `KILL` lets nothing clean up; the next start is a crash recovery for the whole server.

prompt: A nightly job runs `pg_dump shop | gzip > shop.sql.gz`, and when the dump fails the line still exits 0, because a pipeline reports its last program. The script should begin with `set -o ___`.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 1.

prompt: `pg_dump shop > shop.sql` is running in the foreground, and you press `Ctrl+\` to stop it. By the lesson's rule, what does `echo $?` print straight afterwards?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6.

prompt: The database server still runs PostgreSQL 16.2, though `apt upgrade` has run every month without a word about it, and `apt list --upgradable` shows 16.15 waiting. Which command comes first?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 7; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 20.

choices.text: `apt policy postgresql-16`, as priority 100 on the installed version blocks the new one
choices.why: Priority 100 only stops an installed package being replaced by an older one.

choices.text: `pg_upgradecluster`, because going from 16.2 to 16.15 converts the data directory
choices.why: That is a minor release: new programs and a restart, with no file converted.

choices.text: Install 16.3 first and then each later release, since apt cannot skip any
choices.why: Minor releases are cumulative; 16.15 carries every fix since 16.2.

choices.text: `apt-mark showhold`
choices.why: Right: a held package is skipped by every upgrade, silently.

prompt: On a dedicated PostgreSQL server, `free -h` shows about 300 MB under `free`, 10 GB under `buff/cache` and 10 GB under `available`. A colleague wants a nightly job that drops the caches to free memory. What do you answer?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 6.

choices.text: No: that cache is the second one the database reads its pages through
choices.why: Right: dropping it turns its cheap reads into real disk reads.

choices.text: Yes: with 300 MB free, the next large sort will be killed for lack of memory
choices.why: `available` is the number that says what a program can get, and it reads 10 GB.

choices.text: Yes, after raising `shared_buffers` to 12 GB so the server keeps the pages
choices.why: Memory given to one cache is taken from the other; a quarter of the machine is the starting point.

choices.text: No: add swap instead, so that the cache can be moved out to disk
choices.why: Swap parks cold program pages; it is not a place for the file cache, and it fixes no shortage.

prompt: On Monday morning every database session was cut at once. `dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'` shows `Out of memory: Killed process 48211 (postgres)`, and 48211 was one of twenty sessions running the same report. What happened?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 6.

choices.text: The kernel killed the backends one by one, each scoring worst once the last had gone
choices.why: There is one kill in the log; the other sessions were ended by the postmaster.

choices.text: One backend was killed, and the postmaster restarted every other connection to be safe
choices.why: Right: it cannot trust shared memory a killed backend may have left half changed.

choices.text: The report's sorts went past `work_mem`, and the server ended the sessions to free it
choices.why: A sort past `work_mem` spills to temporary files; nothing is ended for it.

choices.text: A `MemoryMax=` on the cluster's unit was reached, and systemd stopped the whole service
choices.why: A limit on a group logs `Memory cgroup out of memory`; this line says the machine ran out.

prompt: Small write transactions have become slow. On the database's NVMe volume, `iostat -xz 2` shows `%util` at 100, `aqu-sz` near 1, `w_await` 0.4 ms and `f_await` 38 ms. What does that say?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 8.

choices.text: The device is saturated, as `%util` shows; spread the tables over a second volume
choices.why: On a device with a queue, `%util` at 100 is a fact, not a verdict on saturation.

choices.text: Flushes take 38 ms, and every commit has to wait for one before it returns
choices.why: Right: a slow `f_await` on a database volume is the most direct sign the disk is too slow for it.

choices.text: Writes wait 0.4 ms, so the disk is fine and the slowness lies in the queries
choices.why: Ordinary writes land in the page cache; a commit waits for the flush, which is the slow part.

choices.text: Set `fsync = off`, so commits stop waiting for the disk to confirm
choices.why: That can leave the cluster corrupt after a power cut; `synchronous_commit` is the one to relax knowingly.

prompt: PostgreSQL's log fills with `No space left on device` for its data volume, and the application has started failing. Which of these belong before anything is deleted? Choose all that apply.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 4.

choices.text: `df -i` on the volume, to see whether the inodes ran out
choices.why: Right: every file needs an inode, and the error names the wrong number when they run out.

choices.text: Delete the oldest segments in `pg_wal`, the largest directory there
choices.why: The server needs those segments to recover after a crash; delete the wrong one and it may not start.

choices.text: `lsof +L1` on the volume, for space held by a file deleted while open
choices.why: Right: that space comes back only when the process holding it closes the file.

choices.text: Remove old log files until `df -h` shows room, then look for the cause
choices.why: If a deleted file still held open is using the space, deleting more achieves nothing.

prompt: From the application server, `nc -zv 10.0.0.7 5432` answers `Connection refused` at once. On the database server, `ss -ltn 'sport = 5432'` shows one line, `127.0.0.1:5432`. What fixes it?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 3; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 5.

choices.text: A `host` line for the application server in `pg_hba.conf`, then a reload
choices.why: That line is the second door; the first is an address the server listens on, which it lacks.

choices.text: `listen_addresses` naming 10.0.0.7, then `systemctl reload postgresql`
choices.why: It is a `postmaster` parameter: a reload leaves it pending until a restart.

choices.text: `listen_addresses` naming 10.0.0.7, then a full restart of PostgreSQL
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A higher `max_connections`, as the server turns new clients away
choices.why: A full server answers `sorry, too many clients already`; a refusal never reached it.

prompt: A new application server tries to reach PostgreSQL, and over a week its log shows four different errors. Match each one to what it says about where the attempt stopped.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 3; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 5.

pairs.right: nothing listening on that address and port, or a reject rule
something on the path silently discarding the attempt
the server was reached, and no line matches the client
a line matched, and the password check did not pass

right_distractors: every connection slot on the server already taken

prompt: The database server keeps `listen_addresses` at `localhost`. From your laptop you run `ssh -f -N -L 6543:127.0.0.1:5432 db`, then `psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 6543 shop`. Which `pg_hba.conf` line decides whether you get in?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 7; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 5.

choices.text: A `host` line for the laptop's own address, which the server has to carry
choices.why: The server never sees the laptop: sshd opens the connection from the server itself.

choices.text: `local all all peer`, since the tunnel ends inside the machine
choices.why: The tunnel ends at `127.0.0.1` port 5432, which is TCP, not the socket.

choices.text: None of them, because what travels inside SSH skips `pg_hba.conf`
choices.why: Every connection meets the file; SSH only changes where it seems to come from.

choices.text: The `host` line for `127.0.0.1/32`
choices.why: Right: sshd on the server connects to `127.0.0.1`, so that is the address the file matches.

prompt: The database servers accept SSH only from the bastion. In `~/.ssh/config`, the `Host db` block gets the line `___ bastion`, so that `ssh db`, `scp` and `rsync` all hop through it.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 7.

prompt: Each night the database server runs `rsync -a --delete /var/lib/pgbackrest/ backup-host:pgbackrest/`, logging in with a key held by its `postgres` account. Why is that offsite copy weaker than it looks?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 8; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 9.

choices.text: Whoever takes this machine also gets to erase the copy, by hand or via the next run
choices.why: Right: an emptied repository is mirrored as empty, and the key itself can delete.

choices.text: The trailing slash makes rsync create `pgbackrest/pgbackrest` on the far side
choices.why: With the slash the contents are copied in; without it the folder itself would be.

choices.text: rsync over SSH sends the backup in the clear for anybody on the path to read
choices.why: rsync over SSH travels inside SSH, encrypted, on port 22.

choices.text: rsync sends only the changed parts, so the far copy is never a whole backup
choices.why: Only the transfer is a difference; what lands on the far side is a complete mirror.

prompt: After a network change, the application server cannot reach `db.example.com` on port 5432. Put the checks in the order the lesson climbs them.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 10.
items: `ip -br addr`, to see the interface is up with an address
`ping` the gateway, the first hop
`ping 10.0.0.7`, the database server's address
`dig db.example.com`, to see what the name answers
`nc -zv 10.0.0.7 5432`, to see whether anything answers on the port
trap: Starting with the database's port is tempting, and a failure there means nothing until every step below it has passed.

prompt: After a failover, `db.example.com` was pointed at the new primary on ns1, and `dig @ns1` shows the new address. The application servers, which all use the company's own resolver, still get the old one with a TTL of 3402 counting down. What brings them over now?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 4; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 19.

choices.text: Lowering the record's TTL on ns1 to 60, so their copies expire within a minute
choices.why: A cached copy keeps the TTL it was given; the new value reaches only the next lookup.

choices.text: Waiting, while the change is propagated outward from ns1 to the resolvers
choices.why: Nothing is sent anywhere: each resolver keeps its answer until the TTL runs out.

choices.text: Raising the zone's serial again, so that every resolver notices the change
choices.why: The serial tells secondary servers the zone changed; resolvers never read it.

choices.text: Flushing that name from the resolver they share, so its next lookup asks ns1
choices.why: Right: resolvers elsewhere still wait out the TTL.

prompt: The lesson's check warns thirty days ahead with `openssl x509 -noout -enddate -checkend 2592000`. You want the same check to warn one week ahead instead. What number goes after `-checkend`?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 6.

prompt: The backup dashboard's certificate was renewed last week, and a check on its server, `openssl x509 -in` the certificate file `-checkend 2592000`, says it will not expire. Since this morning every user, on laptops and phones alike, gets `certificate has expired`. What explains it?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 6.

choices.text: The users' clocks are wrong, and a client's own clock judges the dates
choices.why: One wrong clock explains one machine, not every user on every kind of device.

choices.text: The process serving it never loaded the new file and still sends the old one
choices.why: Right: only a check of what the server sends, through `openssl s_client`, sees that.

choices.text: `-checkend 2592000` looks thirty days ahead and misses a date already passed
choices.why: A certificate already expired fails any `-checkend`; the file checked is simply the new one.

choices.text: The server sends no intermediate, so clients cannot follow the chain to a root
choices.why: A missing intermediate reads `unable to get local issuer certificate`, not `expired`.

prompt: On the application server, `ss -tan state time-wait` lists about three thousand lines whose peer is `10.0.0.7:5432`, the database. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 3; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 10.

choices.text: The database is failing to close its side, a bug in the server's code
choices.why: A side that will not close shows `CLOSE-WAIT`, and on the side that failed to close.

choices.text: Each line is a connection this side closed first, held for 60 seconds
choices.why: Right: so a late packet from it is not taken for part of a new one.

choices.text: They are attempts the database refused, each left in `TIME-WAIT` afterwards
choices.why: A refusal is one SYN and one RST; no connection was ever open to be waited out.

choices.text: The application opens a fresh connection for most of its requests
choices.why: Right: each one costs the server a process start, which a pool would save.

prompt: A session left `idle in transaction` for two days was finally ended, and the next VACUUM of `orders` removed every dead version. The table holds the same live rows as before, yet its file is still twice the size. Why?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 8; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 15.

choices.text: VACUUM marks the space free for new versions and returns only empty pages at the end
choices.why: Right: the file keeps the size it had at its fullest, and shrinking it takes a rewrite.

choices.text: The freed pages go back to the disk at the next checkpoint, when they are written
choices.why: A checkpoint writes dirty pages to their files; it does not cut the files down.

choices.text: Its index entries for dead rows must go first, and only then can the file get smaller
choices.why: VACUUM removed those entries in the same run; the table's file still kept its size.

choices.text: Autovacuum has not been round since, and it is the one that hands space back
choices.why: Autovacuum runs the same VACUUM; it would leave the file the same size.

prompt: At two in the afternoon you are asked which statements are slow on a busy server where `shared_preload_libraries` is empty, and nobody may be disconnected before tonight. What can you start now?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 10; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 18.

choices.text: `ALTER SYSTEM SET shared_preload_libraries`, then `pg_reload_conf()`
choices.why: That list is read only when the server starts, so it waits for tonight's restart.

choices.text: `CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements`, and read the view at once
choices.why: The view is created, but reading it fails until the library has been loaded at start.

choices.text: `ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement`, then `pg_reload_conf()`
choices.why: Right: a reload applies it to every session, and nobody is cut off.

choices.text: `SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset()`, so the counts begin from this moment
choices.why: There are no counts to reset while the library is not loaded; nothing is being collected.

prompt: The shop moved from MySQL 8 to PostgreSQL with pgloader; the copy reported no errors and every row matched. A month later support finds `ana@example.com` and `Ana@example.com` as two accounts, though `email` is `UNIQUE` in both engines. What explains it?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 12; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 21.

choices.text: pgloader left the `UNIQUE` constraint behind, so PostgreSQL never refused the second address
choices.why: Even with it in place, a PostgreSQL `UNIQUE` on the plain column accepts both, because it compares exactly.

choices.text: MySQL's default collation is case-insensitive, so its `UNIQUE` refused one; PostgreSQL compares exactly
choices.why: Right: a unique index on `lower(email)` asks PostgreSQL for the old behaviour, once the pair is merged.

choices.text: The new server folds unquoted values to lower case, as it folds names, so they differ
choices.why: Folding applies to identifiers such as table names; a stored value is kept as written.

choices.text: MySQL's old `utf8` stored the capital letter in a way PostgreSQL reads as a different character
choices.why: The three-byte limit of `utf8` costs emoji; it does not turn a capital into another letter.

prompt: Four orders, in `day` order: day 1 with a total of 12, two on day 2 with totals of 8 and 30, and day 3 with 5. The query computes `sum(total) OVER (ORDER BY day)`, with no frame written. What value does the first day-2 row show?

prompt: `invoices` has eighty million rows, is written all day, and `status` has to become `NOT NULL` without locking the table for more than a moment. Put the steps in order.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 3.

Fill in the existing nulls, in batches
`VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` the check
`ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL`
Drop the check, which has done its job

prompt: A checkout opens a transaction, inserts the order, calls the payment provider over HTTP, which can take thirty seconds, then marks the order paid and commits. What shape does the lesson recommend instead?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 8.

choices.text: Keep the one transaction, and lock the order row with `FOR UPDATE` first
choices.why: That keeps the locks for the provider's thirty seconds, which is the problem itself.

choices.text: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` below thirty seconds
choices.why: That kills the checkouts whose provider is slow; it does not take the wait out of the transaction.

choices.text: Run the transaction at `SERIALIZABLE`, so no other checkout can conflict with it
choices.why: The isolation level does not shorten how long the locks are held.

choices.text: Commit a `pending` row, call the provider, then settle it in a new transaction
choices.why: Right: the slow part sits between two short transactions, and the row says where things stand.

prompt: `customers.last_seen` is set on every request. A developer adds an index on it, in case a report needs one some day. Where does the cost of that index land?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 9.

choices.text: On reads by `id`, which the planner now sends through the new index
choices.why: A lookup by `id` still uses the primary key; nothing about reads moved.

choices.text: Nowhere until the report exists, since an index costs only when it is read
choices.why: An index is maintained on every write for as long as it exists, read or not.

choices.text: On every request's update, which now changes an indexed column
choices.why: Right: the update can no longer skip the index work, so every index gets an entry.

choices.text: On disk alone, since an update of one column touches only that column's index
choices.why: An update writes a new version of the whole row, and every index may need to point at it.

prompt: A raw query must take a list of ids whose length changes from call to call. With one parameter holding the whole array, the condition is written `WHERE id = ___($1)`.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 11.

prompt: `orders` has a primary key on `id` and an index on `(customer_id, created_at)`. Which of these further indexes are pure loss? Choose all that apply.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 9.

choices.text: An index on `(customer_id)`
choices.why: Right: the composite already serves every query this one would.

choices.text: An index on `(created_at)`, for a report filtering on dates alone
choices.why: The composite starts with `customer_id`, so it does nothing for a date on its own.

choices.text: An index on `(id)`, created by hand
choices.why: Right: the primary key is already an index on `id`.

choices.text: An index kept for a report that was deleted last year
choices.why: Right: it is maintained on every write and serves no query.

prompt: A transfer at `SERIALIZABLE` reads two balances, decides how much to move, and updates both. Its commit fails with SQLSTATE `40001`. Why does the retry start again from `BEGIN` rather than re-run the last `UPDATE`?
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 8.

choices.text: What it read is no longer true, so the decision has to be made again from new reads
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The `UPDATE` would hit the same lock cycle again unless a new `BEGIN` reorders it
choices.why: That describes a deadlock; `40001` says the premise of what was read turned out false.

choices.text: `40001` means the row is a genuine duplicate, which only a fresh transaction can see
choices.why: A genuine duplicate is `23505`, and retrying that fails the same way every time.

choices.text: PostgreSQL re-runs the failed statement by itself, so only `COMMIT` is sent
choices.why: After a failure every statement is refused until a rollback; nothing resumes.

prompt: So that a deploy does not run a twenty-minute query while its migration is open, the view is created empty with `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue AS SELECT ... WITH NO ___;` and filled later by a refresh.
hint: Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 7.

prompt: The application reaches PostgreSQL as role `app` through PgBouncer in transaction mode, and its forgotten transactions hold rows for hours. You want any session idle in a transaction for over a minute ended. Where does `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` go?

choices.text: A `SET` the application sends once, when it first connects to PgBouncer
choices.why: A session setting stays on whichever server connection ran it, reaching other clients and missing the rest.

choices.text: `ALTER ROLE app SET`, picked up by each new server connection of `app`
choices.why: Right: the pool's connections log in as `app`, and nobody else is caught.

choices.text: `ALTER SYSTEM`, and a reload, so every session on the server gets it
choices.why: That also ends your own sessions and long maintenance jobs, which the limit was never chosen for.

choices.text: `ALTER DATABASE shop SET`, so only connections to `shop` are limited
choices.why: Your own psql sessions and maintenance jobs in `shop` would be caught by the application's limit too.

prompt: `VACUUM (VERBOSE)` on a busy table keeps reporting `100000 are dead but not yet removable`, yet `pg_stat_activity` shows no session with an old `xact_start`. Which views are worth reading next? Choose all that apply.
hint: Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 14; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 11.

choices.why: It shows how far a running VACUUM has got; it says nothing about who holds old row versions.

choices.text: `pg_prepared_xacts`, for a prepared transaction nobody committed or rolled back
choices.why: Right: it holds the line like a session, and `pg_stat_activity` does not list it.

choices.text: `pg_replication_slots`, for a slot with `active` false whose standby has stopped
choices.why: Right: a slot whose consumer is gone keeps its old `xmin` and holds the line.

prompt: A table's `reltuples` is 3,000,000, and it has been given `ALTER TABLE ... SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01)`, with every other setting at its default. After how many dead row versions does autovacuum vacuum it?
hint: Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 14.

prompt: Each night a job loads 300,000 orders with a new status, and the morning report then crawls. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows the scan of `orders` estimated at `rows=1` and returning `rows=300000`, under a nested loop. What should change in the job?
hint: Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 16; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 10.

choices.text: End it with `ANALYZE orders`, which lets reads and writes carry on
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Raise `work_mem` for the job, so the nested loop has room to run
choices.why: The loop was chosen because the planner expected one row; memory does not change that estimate.

choices.text: Switch autovacuum off on `orders` while it loads, then back on
choices.why: That holds open the window in which the summary is stale; it does not close it.

choices.text: Add an index on `status`, so the report stops scanning the table
choices.why: The plan already scans through an index; what is wrong is the row count it was planned on.

prompt: A migration rewrites `orders_live` to change a column's type, about a minute of work. So that it cannot queue the application behind it, its file starts with `SET statement_timeout = '2s'`. The table is quiet when it runs. What happens?
hint: Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 22; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 3.

choices.text: It waits up to two seconds for its lock, then has the table to itself
choices.why: That is `lock_timeout`, which counts only the wait; this setting counts the work as well.

choices.text: It finishes, because `statement_timeout` does not apply to `ALTER TABLE`
choices.why: It applies to any statement; that is why it cuts a rewrite off halfway.

choices.text: It gets its lock, works for two seconds and is cancelled, every run
choices.why: Right: `lock_timeout` would have limited the wait and let the work finish.

choices.text: It finishes, and the two seconds bound the queries queued after it
choices.why: The setting belongs to the session that set it; the others are not touched.

prompt: Every slot is taken, and even `sudo -u postgres psql` answers `sorry, too many clients already`. A colleague has the pid of one runaway application backend from `ps` and is about to run `sudo kill -9` on it. What should be sent instead, and why?

choices.text: A restart of the service, since a backend ignores `SIGTERM` the way `stubborn.sh` did
choices.why: A backend handles `SIGTERM` and exits cleanly; a restart costs every connection.

choices.text: Nothing else: `-9` frees the one slot, and only that backend's transaction is lost
choices.why: A backend that dies without cleaning up may leave shared memory half changed, and every session pays.

choices.text: `kill -STOP`, which freezes the backend and hands its slot back until a `-CONT`
choices.why: A frozen process still exists and still holds its slot and its locks.

choices.text: Plain `kill`, the `SIGTERM` that `pg_terminate_backend` sends: only that session rolls back
choices.why: Right: a backend killed with `-9` cannot clean up, so the postmaster restarts every process.

prompt: The shop moved from MySQL to PostgreSQL overnight, and every row arrived with the id it had. On the first morning, the first new order is refused because its id collides with an existing row. Which step of the migration was missed?
hint: Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 21.

choices.text: Making `INT UNSIGNED` columns `bigint`, so large ids did not wrap round
choices.why: A value too large for its column is refused at load; it does not wrap onto an id in use.

choices.text: Turning each `0000-00-00` date into NULL before the load
choices.why: That decides what a missing date becomes; it does nothing to how new ids are numbered.

choices.text: Folding `"Customers"` to lower case, so queries without quotes find it
choices.why: A name in the wrong case makes a query fail to find the table, not collide on an id.

choices.text: Starting each sequence after the highest id already copied
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Nobody restarted the Ubuntu server, yet this morning's log shows `received fast shutdown request` and, seconds later, `starting PostgreSQL 16.15`, where the previous start said 16.2. What most likely happened?
hint: Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 20.

choices.text: `apt upgrade` moved the cluster to a new major version, as it does each autumn
choices.why: 16.2 to 16.15 is a minor release, and Ubuntu never changes the major version within a release.

choices.text: The server crashed in the night, and recovery started it on the newer binaries
choices.why: A crash leaves no fast shutdown line, and recovery does not change the programs.

choices.text: unattended-upgrades installed the minor release from the security pocket
choices.why: Right: the package's scripts stopped the cluster, swapped the programs and started it.

choices.text: `pg_upgradecluster` ran from a timer, converting the data directory as it went
choices.why: That is the tool for a major upgrade; a minor release converts nothing.

prompt: To speed up nightly loads, a colleague wants `fsync = off` on the production server. He tested it: ten `kill -9`s on the server under load, and it came back clean every time. What does his test miss?
hint: Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 8.

choices.text: Writes in the operating system's cache survive a kill; a power cut loses them
choices.why: Right: only a power loss or a kernel crash shows what `fsync = off` costs.

choices.text: Nothing: a clean recovery after a kill shows the order of writes still holds
choices.why: Nothing enforces that order with `fsync` off; the kill simply never put it to the test.

choices.text: Recovery replays the log, which is still flushed, so only table files are at risk
choices.why: With `fsync` off the call is not made for the log either.

choices.text: `kill -9` sends `SIGTERM` first, so the server had time to flush before it died
choices.why: `SIGKILL` cannot be caught and asks nothing; there is no warning to flush on.

prompt: A migration runs `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS orders_one_per_customer ON orders (customer_id)`. The first deploy failed on a duplicated key. The re-run printed `already exists, skipping` and then `CREATE INDEX`. What is true now?

choices.text: An invalid index left by the first run holds the name, and no query uses it
choices.why: Right: `pg_index` shows it with `indisvalid` false; drop it, fix the data, and run it without `IF NOT EXISTS`.

choices.text: The first run's index finished building in the background once the duplicate was skipped
choices.why: A build that found a duplicate stops; nothing completes it later.

choices.text: Nothing is left of the first run, because a failed statement rolls back whole
choices.why: That is the plain `CREATE INDEX`; the concurrent one had already committed its first step.

prompt: A server that matters is on 16.2, and Ubuntu has 16.15 waiting. Put the minor upgrade in order.

Read the Migration section of every release note in between

`sudo apt install postgresql-16`

prompt: On a server where `max_prepared_transactions` is 0, `VACUUM (VERBOSE)` prints a `removable cutoff` millions of XIDs old. `~/oldest.sql` returns no rows, and `pg_wal` has been growing for days. Where do you look next?
hint: Database Performance and Scale, lesson 15; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 11.

choices.text: `pg_stat_archiver`, since a failing archive command holds back VACUUM too
choices.why: A broken archive keeps segments in pg_wal, but it holds no snapshot, so it cannot hold the cutoff.

choices.text: `pg_replication_slots`, for a slot whose consumer has gone away
choices.why: Right: a forgotten slot holds both the horizon and the log, and has no row in pg_stat_activity.

choices.text: `pg_prepared_xacts`, for a two-phase commit a coordinator forgot
choices.why: With max_prepared_transactions at 0 there can be none, and one would not make pg_wal grow.

choices.text: `pg_stat_activity` again, sorted by `xact_start` instead of age
choices.why: oldest.sql already lists every session with an xid or a snapshot; sorting differently finds no new one.

prompt: The forgotten transaction has been ended and `VACUUM` has run, but `products` is still more than three times its old size. The shop cannot stop reads or writes on it during the day. What gives the space back?

choices.text: Nothing: the table shrinks by itself as autovacuum catches up
choices.why: The free space is reused by later updates, so the table stops growing; it does not shrink back on its own.

choices.text: `VACUUM FULL`, which writes the live rows into a new, compact file
choices.why: It does compact the table, but it holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole rewrite, which stops even a plain SELECT.

choices.text: Another plain `VACUUM`, now that nothing holds the horizon back
choices.why: Plain VACUUM turns dead versions into free space inside the pages; it hands back only empty pages at the end of the file.

choices.text: `pg_repack`, which locks the table only briefly at each end
choices.why: Right.

prompt: In lesson 15 the pricing robot made about 4650 updates a second on `products`. Had Session A's `REPEATABLE READ` transaction stayed open for 10 minutes at that rate, about how many dead versions would `VACUUM` have had to keep?

prompt: The shop's only standby is also its failover target. So that the hour-long nightly export there stops being cancelled, somebody sets `max_standby_streaming_delay` to two hours on it and leaves `hot_standby_feedback` off. What does that trade away?

choices.text: Dead rows pile up in the primary's busiest tables while the export runs

choices.text: Every commit on the primary waits until the standby has replayed it
choices.why: The standby is asynchronous; holding its replay back never delays a commit on the primary.

choices.text: It falls hours behind during the export, the worst state to promote it from

choices.text: Nothing, since replay catches up at full speed once the export ends

choices.text: Port 5001 refuses a `SELECT`, as standbys take only replication connections

choices.text: Port 5001 sends each connection to whichever node is the primary now
choices.why: That is port 5000; port 5001 spreads connections over the replicas.

choices.text: Superuser pools fill the reserved slots too, leaving no way in to fix it

choices.text: Superusers skip `max_connections`, so the server could run out of memory

choices.why: It counts attempts since the statistics were reset, so a failure fixed long ago keeps it above zero.

choices.why: Right: it is the one that predicts a full disk and a stopped server.

choices.text: On a quiet server, `last_archived_time` is older than `archive_timeout`
choices.why: Right: it catches a command that hangs instead of failing.

prompt: The primary has `synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'`, and standby1 has died. The application's role has `statement_timeout = '3s'`, yet its inserts hang for minutes. Why does the timeout not end them?
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 12; Database Performance and Scale, lesson 15.

choices.text: The statement is finished; what waits is the commit, outside it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A role's setting reaches only new sessions, and these opened earlier
choices.why: That is true of ALTER ROLE, but lesson 12 set the timeout on the session itself and it still waited.

choices.text: Waiting sessions need `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` instead
choices.why: These sessions are active, waiting on SyncRep, and the idle timeout never touches an active session.

choices.text: It fired, but the error is held until the standby comes back
choices.why: Nothing fired: the commit wait lies outside every statement, so no statement limit covers it.

prompt: A standby whose slot was lost should fetch the missing log from pgBackRest. Its log alternates `requested WAL segment 000000010000000000000012 has already been removed` with `ERROR: [032]: PostgreSQL working directory '/var/lib/postgresql/16/standby' is not the same as option pg1-path '/var/lib/postgresql/16/main'`. What fixes it?
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 13.

choices.text: Add `--pg1-path` with the standby's own path to `restore_command`
choices.why: Right: pgBackRest checks that the server asking is the data directory it was told about.

choices.text: Raise `max_slot_wal_keep_size` on the primary and restart the standby
choices.why: The segments are already gone from the primary; a bigger cap helps only the next outage.

choices.text: Rebuild the standby from a new base backup, since the slot is lost
choices.why: That was lesson 11's ending; with the archive beside the slot, the standby catches up without one.

choices.text: Run `stanza-create` again so that the standby joins the stanza
choices.why: The stanza is fine and the archive holds the segments; only the command fetching them was refused.

prompt: To be ready for `pg_rewind`, you ran `ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_log_hints = on` on the primary and restarted it. On the standby, `SHOW wal_log_hints` still answers `off`. Why?
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 15; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 5.

choices.text: The standby received the value but waits for a restart, as `pending_restart` would show
choices.why: Nothing reached the standby to be pending; the file that changed is the primary's.

choices.text: A line in the standby's `conf.d` overrides the value replication brought
choices.why: postgresql.auto.conf is read last and wins over conf.d; here the value never arrived at all.

choices.text: Physical replication applies settings only at the standby's next checkpoint
choices.why: It carries the log of data changes, never configuration files, at any checkpoint.

choices.text: The command wrote `postgresql.auto.conf` on the primary alone, and no file is replicated
choices.why: Right: set it on the standby too, and restart it there.

prompt: The writes have been stopped for maintenance, and the role of primary is to move to the standby without losing anything. Put the rest of the switchover in the order lesson 15 gives.
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 15.
items: Stop the primary cleanly
Confirm the standby has replayed past the primary's last checkpoint
Promote the standby
Make the old primary a standby of the new one, and start it
Point the application at the new primary
trap: Promoting before the old primary has stopped cleanly turns a switchover into a failover, with two primaries possible and no proof that nothing was lost.

prompt: A reporting standby, `standby2`, streams from `standby1`, not from the primary. With `hot_standby_feedback = on` set on `standby2` alone, its long reports are still cancelled with `conflict with recovery`. What is missing?
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 20.

choices.text: A larger `max_standby_streaming_delay` set on the primary
choices.why: That setting governs the standby running the query; on the primary it decides nothing.

choices.text: The same setting on `standby1`, so that it passes the request up
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Running the reports at `REPEATABLE READ`, so their snapshot is kept
choices.why: The report already holds one snapshot; that is exactly what the primary's VACUUM removes rows under.

choices.text: A slot for `standby2` on the primary, beside the one on `standby1`
choices.why: standby2 holds its slot on standby1, its source; feedback travels up the chain, step by step.

prompt: `nightly-backup.sh` ran from the `postgres` crontab on a cloud image with no mail transfer agent. A rebuild of the machine left the crontab out, and three weeks went by without a backup. What would have caught it within a day?
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 5; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13.

choices.text: A `MAILTO=ops@example.com` line at the top of the crontab
choices.why: A job that never runs prints nothing to mail, and this machine has nowhere to send mail anyway.

choices.text: Checking the exit status of `pgbackrest verify` inside the job
choices.why: verify exits 0 even on damage, and on a night the job never runs there is no status to read.

choices.text: A monitor elsewhere that expects the job's success report each night
choices.why: Right: only something outside the machine notices a job that never ran.

choices.text: A daily `grep CRON /var/log/syslog` on the rebuilt machine
choices.why: The log lists jobs cron started; a job missing from the crontab leaves no line to find.

prompt: Patroni runs with `synchronous_mode`. The old leader's Patroni froze, another node took over, and inserts still reaching the old primary hang. To tidy up, somebody runs `pg_cancel_backend` on every session waiting there. What has that done?
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 17.

choices.text: Rolled each insert back, because the cancel arrived before its commit
choices.why: They had committed locally before they began to wait, and a cancel cannot take a commit back.

choices.text: Nothing harmful: the rows reach the new leader when the old primary rejoins
choices.why: On rejoining, the old primary is rewound to where the histories split, and what it wrote after is thrown away.

choices.text: Demoted the old primary, since nothing on it waits for a standby now
choices.why: Only its frozen Patroni could demote it; cancelling sessions changes nothing about its role.

choices.text: Told each client its insert worked, on a row the rewind will later throw away
choices.why: Right: the fence was the wait, and cancelling it makes confirmed writes that only the old primary has.

prompt: A colleague remembers the bad `DELETE` as happening at about 14:03, and nobody has read the log yet. Restoring by time with `--target-action=pause`, which way should you err?
hint: Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 6.

choices.text: Exactly 14:03, since people remember the database server's clock
choices.why: The time people remember comes from screens and graphs, not necessarily the server's clock or time zone.

choices.text: Later: a target past the mistake can still be paused before its commit
choices.why: recovery_target_time stops before the first commit after the time given, so a late target replays the DELETE.

choices.text: Earlier: the repair copies back the good transactions it misses
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Either way, because `--target-exclusive` undoes the target's transaction
choices.why: target-exclusive decides whether the named target is replayed; it undoes nothing that comes after it.

prompt: A database container's volume has held data since last year. To rotate the password, the team edits `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and recreates the container, and the new password gets `password authentication failed for user "postgres"`. What changes it without leaving it in a log or a history file?
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 9; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 11.

choices.text: `\password postgres` in psql inside it, as the variable only acts on an empty volume
choices.why: Right: the old password is stored in the database, and `\password` sends a verifier rather than the password.

choices.text: A script in `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` that sets it, run at the next start
choices.why: Setup scripts run only when the data directory is empty, which this volume has not been since last year.

choices.text: `docker exec db psql -c "ALTER ROLE postgres PASSWORD '...'"`, as the variable only acts on an empty volume
choices.why: The reason is right, and the statement carries the password into shell history and, on any error, the server log.

choices.text: Running `docker rm -f db` and the same `docker run` once more, so the change is picked up
choices.why: That is what the team already did; recreating the container leaves the volume, and the password in it, as they were.

prompt: The shop's database runs from `postgres:16` with its data in the named volume `pgdata`. A colleague changes the image to `postgres:17` and starts a new container on the same volume. What happens?
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 8; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 20.

choices.text: 17 converts the volume's files on its first start, so all that is needed is a backup beforehand
choices.why: No version converts another's files on start; something has to carry the data across.

choices.text: 17 refuses those files; pg_upgrade, dump and restore, or logical replication has to move the data
choices.why: Right: a new image is a new major version, and the volume keeps 16's format.

choices.text: It runs as before, because the entrypoint finds a database and skips initialisation
choices.why: Skipping initialisation is true, and the server it then starts cannot read files that 16 wrote.

choices.text: It runs as before, as 16 and 17 share the on-disk format that every minor release keeps unchanged
choices.why: Only minor releases keep the format; a major version changes the system catalogue.

prompt: Every night, while the database runs, a job archives its volume with `docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data:ro -v /srv/backup:/backup alpine:3.22 tar -czf /backup/pgdata.tar.gz -C /data .`, and `/srv/backup` is on the same machine. What keeps this from being a backup the track would accept? Choose all that apply.
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 8; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 9.

choices.text: PostgreSQL may be halfway through writing the files that `tar` copies
choices.why: Right: a running database's files are not a consistent copy.

choices.text: The `:ro` mount stops `tar` from reading the files in the volume
choices.why: Read-only stops the job from changing the volume; reading it is exactly what it allows.

choices.text: The archive sits on the same machine as the database it protects
choices.why: Right: one failure of that machine takes the database and the copy together.

choices.text: The archive ends up owned by `root`, so it cannot be restored
choices.why: Ownership is an inconvenience the lesson fixes later; root can read and restore it like any file.

prompt: Bruno has recreated his database container a dozen times with `docker rm -f db` and the same `docker run`, never naming a volume for `postgres:17`. To free space he runs `docker volume prune`. What happened to the tables his earlier containers held?
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 7.

choices.text: They are safe until the `postgres:17` image itself is removed
choices.why: A volume does not belong to the image; removing the image would not touch it either way.

choices.text: They were already gone, removed with each container's writable layer
choices.why: The image declares its data directory as a volume, so the tables were never in the writable layer.

choices.text: They are safe, because plain `prune` only removes volumes with no files in them
choices.why: Plain `prune` removes anonymous volumes no container uses, full or empty.

choices.text: They are gone: each sat in an anonymous volume nothing was using
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A setup script starts a fresh `postgres:17` container, loops on `docker exec db pg_isready -U postgres -q` until it succeeds, then connects through the published port. The first run fails with `server closed the connection unexpectedly`. Why?
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 9.

choices.text: A temporary server, listening only on a Unix socket, answered the check
choices.why: Right: the entrypoint runs it for the setup scripts and stops it, so the check should ask over TCP.

choices.text: The published port opens a few seconds after the server inside starts
choices.why: Publishing is set up with the container; what was missing was the real server behind the port.

choices.text: `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` is applied after the first connection, which is refused
choices.why: The password is set before the server starts; the failure was not about authentication.

choices.text: The server refuses the host until the port is published on every address
choices.why: Publishing on `127.0.0.1` reaches the server from the host; a check over TCP then connects that way.

prompt: Bruno runs PostgreSQL in a container started with `--memory 2g` on a 16 GB host, and wants `shared_buffers` at the database course's quarter of the machine. What should he size it from?
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 17; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 6.

choices.text: The host's 16 GB, as the kernel only slows a container that goes past its limit
choices.why: Slowing down is what a CPU limit does; at a memory limit the out-of-memory killer ends the process.

choices.text: The host's 16 GB, as shared memory is left out of a container's memory count
choices.why: Nothing in either course leaves the cache outside the limit; it is memory the server allocates like any other.

choices.text: The 2 GB limit, which `docker stats` shows under `MEM USAGE / LIMIT`
choices.why: Right: the cgroup is the server's machine now, so a quarter of it is 512 MB.

choices.text: The host's 16 GB, since the server inside sees the host and plans for it
choices.why: What the server can see is not what it may use; the kernel enforces the 2 GB.

hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 9.

sets the password
runs your setup scripts
starts the server

prompt: A PostgreSQL server keeps its data directory on one `gp3` volume and its write-ahead log on another. A nightly schedule snapshots each volume on its own, a few hundred milliseconds apart. What makes such a pair something the server can be started from?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 5; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 3.

choices.text: Running `fsfreeze` on each volume just before its own snapshot
choices.why: A freeze makes one volume clean at the filesystem level; it does not make two volumes the same moment.

choices.text: One atomic group snapshot, or `pg_backup_start` and `pg_backup_stop` around them
choices.why: Right: either the storage takes both at one instant, or PostgreSQL hands back a `backup_label` that lets the log repair the gap.

choices.text: Copying both snapshots to another region as soon as they finish
choices.why: That answers where the copies live, not whether the two describe the same instant.

choices.text: Snapshotting only the data volume, since the server writes a fresh log when it starts
choices.why: The log is what crash recovery replays; a data copy without its matching log has nothing to recover from.

prompt: A manager wants the standby in Virginia made synchronous, so that losing São Paulo loses nothing. A nightly import commits one million rows one at a time. Using only the floor the lesson worked out from São Paulo to Virginia, at least how many hours of waiting does the standby add to that import?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 9; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 12.

prompt: Your PostgreSQL primary runs in `sa-east-1a` with a standby in `sa-east-1b`, and the application finds the primary through a DNS record that the failover runbook edits. On the day zone a fails, `us-east-1` has a control-plane problem. Which arrangement would have let the application reach the promoted standby anyway?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 9; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 19.

choices.text: Both hosts in the connection string, with `target_session_attrs=read-write`
choices.why: Right: the driver finds the new primary itself, and nothing has to be changed anywhere.

choices.text: A TTL of a few seconds on the record, so that the edited answer reaches clients sooner
choices.why: A short TTL only speeds up an edit that has been made; the edit is the step that goes through Virginia.

choices.text: A virtual IP that `keepalived` moves from zone a to zone b
choices.why: An address that moves between machines needs a network that allows it, which most clouds do not.

choices.text: A runbook step that launches a fresh primary in zone b from a snapshot
choices.why: A new instance has a new address, so the application still waits on the same DNS edit to find it.

prompt: At 14:05 a developer drops a table on a managed PostgreSQL. You start a point-in-time restore to 14:04. What do you have when it finishes?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 5; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 21.

choices.text: The same instance at its usual address, rewound to the state of 14:04
choices.why: A restore does not rewind anything in place; it builds a copy from the backups.

choices.text: The same instance, with the dropped table back and every later write kept in place
choices.why: Point-in-time recovery stops at one moment; nothing after 14:04 is in the copy, and nothing is merged.

choices.text: A new instance with its own address; the old one runs on, table still gone
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A snapshot id, to attach as a volume to the database still running
choices.why: A managed restore hands back a database, and the old one keeps running beside it.

prompt: A new reporting server in the same VPC runs `psql` against the PostgreSQL instance's private address, and you try four broken setups in turn. Match each thing `psql` reports to its cause.

no `host` line matches the reporting server's address

prompt: A nightly `pg_dump` job on the database server uploads to a bucket through a role whose policy allows `s3:*` on `*`. You want the dumps to survive somebody who takes over that server and its role. Which change does that?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 7; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 9.

choices.text: Swap the role for an access key in the job's config file, and rotate it every month
choices.why: A key in a file travels with every copy of the disk, and it can still delete whatever the policy allows.

choices.text: Keep `s3:*`, but narrow `Resource` down to the backup bucket's own ARN
choices.why: Every S3 action on that bucket still includes deleting the dumps in it.

choices.text: Encrypt each dump before upload, with a key kept on the database server
choices.why: Encryption decides who can read a backup; it does nothing about who can delete it.

choices.text: Allow only `s3:PutObject` on the prefix, and leave expiry to a lifecycle rule
choices.why: Right: the server can write new dumps and cannot remove old ones.

prompt: For speed, a test PostgreSQL keeps its data directory on the instance store of an `m7gd.large`. Which of these leaves that data where it was?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 4.

choices.text: Stopping it over the weekend and starting it on Monday
choices.why: A stop releases the host, and the instance store stays behind, erased.

choices.text: A reboot to load a new kernel
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Terminating it with the root volume set to be kept
choices.why: Keeping the root volume saves a network volume; the instance store goes with the instance.

choices.text: A stop and start to move it to a larger instance type
choices.why: Changing the type needs a stop, and a stop erases the instance store.

prompt: PostgreSQL on a 200 GB `gp3` volume commits slowly at peak, and `pg_test_fsync` shows the volume's flushes are the limit. Which change goes at that limit?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 5; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 9.

choices.text: Buying more IOPS for the same `gp3` volume, without changing its size
choices.why: Right: commits wait on how many flushes a second the disk does, and `gp3` sells operations apart from size.

choices.text: Moving the data directory to `st1`, which streams long reads faster for less
choices.why: `st1` is built for long sequential reads and is slow at many small operations.

choices.text: Growing the volume to 400 GB, since a bigger `gp3` does more operations a second
choices.why: That was true of older volume types; `gp3` keeps the same baseline at any size.

choices.text: Buying more throughput in MiB/s, the figure a large file copy shows
choices.why: Throughput is bytes a second of long writes; a commit waits on one small flush at a time.

prompt: A design that already runs enough capacity in its second zone, so that losing the first needs no control-plane call at all, has what AWS's guidance calls static ___.

prompt: A PostgreSQL instance with a 20 GB `gp3` root volume and a fixed public IPv4 address is stopped for a month while a project is on hold. Which of these are still billed during that month? Choose all that apply.
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 4.

choices.why: Right: the volume waits for the instance and bills while it waits.

choices.text: The processor, by the second, as long as the instance exists
choices.why: The processor charge stops with a stop and starts again with a start.

choices.text: The instance store disks, until the instance is terminated
choices.why: Instance store is part of the instance's price, and a stopped instance pays none of it.

choices.text: The fixed public IPv4 address kept for it
choices.why: Right: keeping an address fixed is a resource of its own, billed by the hour.

prompt: A colleague tests a Redis running `appendfsync no`: some writes, a `docker kill`, a restart, and nothing is missing. They conclude it is as safe as `always`. Which PostgreSQL finding is the same trap?
hint: NoSQL: Modelling and Operations, lesson 13; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 8.

choices.text: An `UNLOGGED` table coming back empty after a `docker kill` and restart
choices.why: That test did show a loss; the trap is a test that cannot show one.

choices.text: `synchronous_commit = off` roughly doubling the work done in thirty seconds of `pgbench`
choices.why: That is a measurement of speed, not a crash test that hides what a power cut would cost.

choices.text: `fsync = off` passing every `kill -9`, since the kernel still writes its cache out
choices.why: Right: a killed process leaves the page cache behind, so only a power cut or a kernel crash shows what is lost.

choices.text: `statement_timeout` failing to end a commit that waits on `SyncRep`
choices.why: That is a defence that does not bound a wait; nothing about it hides a loss from a test.

prompt: A shop reads its "my orders" page with read preference `secondaryPreferred` to spare the primary, on a replica set of three. Customers who have just placed an order, written with `w: 1`, sometimes see no order and place it again. The PostgreSQL team met the same complaint with a read replica. Which fix do both courses give first?
hint: NoSQL: Modelling and Operations, lesson 9; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 13.

choices.text: Write orders with `w: "majority"` and keep reading from any secondary
choices.why: A majority of three is the primary and one secondary; the read can still land on the other one.

choices.text: Keep `secondaryPreferred` and add `readConcern("majority")` to that read
choices.why: `"majority"` buys durability, not freshness: it can return something older than the member's own latest.

choices.text: Switch the page to `nearest`, which picks whichever member answers fastest
choices.why: The fastest member may well be a secondary that has not caught up.

choices.text: Send that page's reads to the primary for a while after each new order
choices.why: Right: the primary is the only place guaranteed to have the write it just acknowledged.

prompt: Two primaries are each cut off from everything but one client: a Redis with `min-replicas-to-write 1` and `min-replicas-max-lag 10`, and a PostgreSQL leader under Patroni's `synchronous_mode`, whose synchronous standby now follows the new leader. How do the writes each of them confirms differ?
hint: NoSQL: Modelling and Operations, lesson 15; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 17.

choices.text: Both refuse from the first write, as each one needs a replica to answer
choices.why: Redis counts a replica as good for up to ten seconds after it last answered, so it accepts writes until then.

choices.text: Redis says `OK` for its first seconds and loses those writes; PostgreSQL confirms none
choices.why: Right: the Redis setting bounds the window without closing it, while every PostgreSQL commit waits for a standby it no longer has.

choices.text: Redis refuses at once with `NOREPLICAS`; PostgreSQL confirms writes until its key expires
choices.why: That is the wrong way round on both sides: the lag has to pass first, and the commit waits on the standby, not on the key.

choices.text: Both confirm every write, and the two histories are merged when the network heals
choices.why: Neither merges anything: the old Redis primary flushes its data on rejoining, and PostgreSQL never confirmed its writes.

prompt: The shop's MongoDB has grown to 400 GB, with six indexes on its largest collection, and the signed RTO is one hour. The last drill, a `mongorestore` of the 100,000-order lab copy, finished in under two seconds. What should the team conclude?

choices.text: Nothing yet: time the restore again, on a full copy of the real data and indexes
choices.why: Right: rebuilding the indexes grows with the data times their number, and only a measurement says whether it fits.

choices.text: The hour is met with room to spare, as a restore grows only with the bytes copied
choices.why: That is how a snapshot's restore grows; a dump's restore inserts every document and builds every index again.

choices.text: A file snapshot would take just as long, since both restores insert every document
choices.why: A snapshot is restored by starting a server on the files; its indexes are already there.

choices.text: Rerun the drill on a smaller server, since the hardware does not change the time
choices.why: A restore is measured on the hardware that will do it; a smaller server is slower, not a fair stand-in.
