prompt: Which of these lose writes that Redis had already acknowledged? Choose all that apply.
hint: NoSQL: Modelling and Operations, lesson 13.

choices.text: `appendfsync everysec`, and the process is killed
choices.why: The kernel keeps the bytes `write()` handed it and flushes them after the process dies.

choices.text: `appendfsync everysec`, and the machine loses power
choices.why: Right: about the last second, which had not been flushed yet.

choices.text: Snapshots only, and the process is killed
choices.why: Right: every write since the last snapshot is gone.

choices.text: `appendfsync always`, and the machine loses power
choices.why: Each write is flushed before the reply, so nothing acknowledged is lost.

prompt: After a month of normal traffic, on a MongoDB that has not restarted and serves every read from the primary, `$indexStats` shows zero operations for `email_1`, a unique index, and for `items.sku_1`. What does a careful cleanup do?
hint: NoSQL: Modelling and Operations, lesson 7; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 9.

choices.text: Drop `email_1`, keep `items.sku_1`, since the application already checks for duplicates
choices.why: Two inserts checked at the same moment both see no duplicate; only the index makes one per e-mail true.

choices.text: Drop both, since a month of zero on the member taking every read is enough evidence
choices.why: A unique index has a second job, refusing duplicates, which no read ever counts.

choices.text: Keep both, since `$indexStats` counts only `explain()` runs and not real queries
choices.why: It is the other way round: real operations are counted and `explain()` calls are not.

choices.text: Drop `items.sku_1` and keep `email_1`
choices.why: Right: the unique index enforces one account per e-mail without any query ever searching it.

prompt: A managed Redis set to `allkeys-lru` reaches its memory limit and silently evicts carts that existed nowhere else. The provider's status page shows nothing wrong. Whose decision caused the loss?
hint: NoSQL: Modelling and Operations, lesson 21.

choices.text: The provider's, since data lost on a managed service is an outage it must answer for
choices.why: The provider ran the policy it was given; an eviction it was told to make is not its outage.

choices.text: The team's: which keys are allowed to be evicted is a choice about their own data
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A failover's, whose dropped connections a retry in the application would have saved
choices.why: No failover happened; the keys were evicted on purpose by the policy.

choices.text: The maintenance window's, since its patching restarted the instance empty
choices.why: A restart is not what removed them; the policy evicted them while the instance kept running.

prompt: The shop's application connects as `app`, which also owns `customers` and `orders` so that migrations can run under it. A review finds an injection flaw in the application. Which change most limits what the flaw can do?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 6; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 12.

choices.text: Revoke the right to drop tables from `app` and leave it as the owner
choices.why: Ownership cannot be limited by a grant: whoever owns a table can alter, drop and grant on it.

choices.text: Require a second factor whenever the `app` role logs in
choices.why: The flaw runs inside a session the application has already opened; a factor guards the login, not what follows.

choices.text: Give the tables to a `NOLOGIN` owner; grant `app` row privileges only
choices.why: Right: an injected statement can then lose rows, which a backup brings back, but cannot drop a table.

choices.text: Rename `app` to something no attacker could guess from outside
choices.why: The injected statement runs as whatever role the application uses; its name hides nothing from it.

prompt: Four things happen on the shop's PostgreSQL server. Match each one to the question of access control it answers.
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 8; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 11.

pairs.left: `psql -U app` naming the role to log in as
pairs.right: identification

pairs.left: the server checking the password against the role's SCRAM verifier
pairs.right: authentication

pairs.left: only a superuser being allowed to read `pg_authid`
pairs.right: authorisation

pairs.left: the server log keeping a failed `ALTER ROLE` and who sent it
pairs.right: accounting

prompt: A plan counts two layers against losing the shop's data: the database, and an offsite pgBackRest repository that `postgres` on the database server pushes to every night. Why would the security lesson count them as one layer?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 4; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 9.

choices.text: A single break-in as `postgres` there reaches the backups and the data alike
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The repository sits on other storage, so the two already fail for different reasons
choices.why: Other storage survives a dead disk; it does not survive the one cause that can reach both.

choices.text: A backup only notices damage, so it cannot count as a layer at all
choices.why: Restoring from backup is a corrective control; it counts whenever it fails for its own reasons.

choices.text: Both are written by PostgreSQL, so a bug in one version reaches both
choices.why: The repository is written by pgBackRest; the shared cause here is a credential, not the software.

prompt: Each month ana restores the nightly `pg_dump` of `shop` into a second database on the same server, and the rows match the live ones. The yearly walk-through restores on a different machine instead. What would that restore show here?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 12; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 2.

choices.text: Nothing new, since a dump that matches row for row on one server matches on any
choices.why: The same-server test found everything the dump assumed already there; a new server has none of it.

choices.text: That the archive's SHA-256 changes once it is copied to another machine
choices.why: A digest changes only when bytes change; an intact copy checks `OK` anywhere.

choices.text: That no roles travel in the dump, so its ownership and grants fail there
choices.why: Right: roles belong to the whole server, and `pg_restore` reports each line naming one.

choices.text: That the dump holds the old data directory's path, which a new server lacks
choices.why: A logical dump is statements and rows; it names no file paths.

prompt: A developer proposes keeping a nightly copy of the orders on `www`, in the DMZ, so that the shop's pages load without asking `db`. What does the lesson say?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 5.

choices.text: Fine if the copy is read-only, since the DMZ is behind a firewall too
choices.why: `www` is the server most likely to be compromised, and read-only data is still readable by an intruder.

choices.text: The orders stay in `db`, and `www` asks through the one allowed port
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Better to move `db` into the DMZ as well, so both share one zone
choices.why: That would let the internet reach the zone holding the data; the DMZ is for what must answer the internet.

choices.text: Keep the copy outside the firewall, where it cannot reach the inside
choices.why: Outside the firewall nothing protects it, and anybody on the internet can reach it.

prompt: On the shop's server, `\du` shows ana's own role as `Superuser, Create role, Create DB`, and she uses it every day to run the sales reports. What does the security lesson recommend?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 6; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 11.

choices.text: Nothing needs changing: she is trusted, and the role is hers alone
choices.why: Least privilege limits the damage of anything that goes wrong while acting as her, not her honesty.

choices.text: A second person approving each report before she runs it
choices.why: That is separation of duties for a sensitive task; the problem here is a standing privilege behind routine work.

choices.text: Changing her password every month, so a leaked one dies soon
choices.why: A stolen password still works fully until it changes; what matters is how far the role reaches.

choices.text: An ordinary role for daily work; the powerful one kept for administration
choices.why: Right.

prompt: ana is the shop's only DBA. She writes every schema change and applies it herself, and nobody else can review a change before it runs. What does the security lesson put in place of that second person?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 6; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 19.

choices.text: `log_statement = 'all'`, so that every statement she sends is kept for review
choices.why: That buries the changes under every `BEGIN` and `END`, and writes literals such as passwords into the file.

choices.text: A role for her that cannot run `DROP`, so that a mistaken change is refused
choices.why: That limits an account; the task still needs somebody able to change the schema, and she is the one.

choices.text: `log_statement = 'ddl'`, in a log the owners read every week
choices.why: Right: the separation becomes detective rather than preventive, and the second person arrives afterwards.

choices.text: Job rotation, handing the schema to a developer every other month
choices.why: Rotation finds frauds that need somebody present every day; with one DBA there is nobody to rotate to.

prompt: Ransomware has taken root on the shop's database server. Which of these backup copies can it destroy from there? Choose all that apply.
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 12; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 9.

choices.text: A bucket under S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
choices.why: The lock refuses deletion before the retention date whatever credential asks, the account's administrator included.

choices.text: A backup disk that stays mounted on the database server
choices.why: Right: whatever the server can write to falls with the server.

choices.text: The weekly encrypted disk that one of the owners takes home
choices.why: A disk on a shelf at somebody's house is offline; no network attack reaches it.

choices.text: A repository directory on that server, marked `chattr +i`
choices.why: Right: root removes the flag as easily as it set it.

prompt: An attacker on a staff laptop who moves on to the database at port 5432 never crosses the perimeter. Traffic between machines inside the network, like this, is called ___ traffic.
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 5.

prompt: The owners decide the orders may lose at most one hour of data and may be down for a whole day. The team proposes keeping the nightly backup and buying storage that restores it in twenty minutes. What does the lesson make of the plan?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 12.

choices.text: It meets both targets, since twenty minutes is well inside a day
choices.why: Twenty minutes answers the RTO; the RPO asks how often, and a nightly backup can lose a day.

choices.text: It pays for speed nobody asked for, and the one hour stays unmet
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It meets the RPO, because a restore that quick loses under an hour
choices.why: How fast a restore runs decides the downtime, not how much the last backup holds.

choices.text: It is sound, as the two targets are one figure and the shorter wins
choices.why: The lesson keeps them independent; treating them as one is exactly how money goes to the wrong one.

prompt: A clinic's `diagnosis` column was filled with pgcrypto's `encrypt(code, key, 'aes')`. An analyst with no key runs `SELECT encode(diagnosis, 'hex'), count(*) FROM patients GROUP BY 1`. What can the result reveal?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 14; Relational Databases and SQL, lesson 6.

choices.text: Which rows hold the same code, and how large each such group is
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing, as every value is random bytes to somebody without the key
choices.why: `encrypt` with `'aes'` uses CBC with an all-zero IV, so equal codes give equal bytes.

choices.text: The codes themselves, since CBC with a zero IV decrypts without a key
choices.why: A fixed IV makes equal inputs look equal; it does not hand back the plaintext.

choices.text: The key's length, read off the size of each ciphertext in the group
choices.why: The size follows the value padded to AES blocks; the key does not show in it.

prompt: The offsite pgBackRest repository is encrypted, and its `repo2-cipher-pass` exists in one place: `/etc/pgbackrest.conf` on the database server. Where else should it be kept?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 14; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 9.

choices.text: Only in the memory of the DBA who generated it, so it sits on no disk at all
choices.why: Then a restore depends on one person being reachable, and no drill can prove the copy is right.

choices.text: In a file beside the backups in the offsite repository, so a restore finds it
choices.why: A key is never stored beside what it protects: whoever takes the repository takes the key.

choices.text: In the configuration repository with `postgresql.conf`, so provisioning rebuilds it
choices.why: A key in a repository is read by everybody who clones it, for as long as any copy exists.

choices.text: In a vault the organisation trusts, open to more than one person, and proved by a drill
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The `app_users` table holds bcrypt values that begin `$2a$06$`. New hashes are to be made with `gen_salt('bf', 12)`. Counting bcrypt's cost the way the lessons define it, how many times as many rounds of key setup does one new hash take as one old hash?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 5; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 18.

prompt: The application's `app_users` rows are bcrypt at cost 06, and the policy is now cost 12, with no forced reset. Put in order what the application does when a user signs in with the right password.
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 5; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 18.
items: Read the algorithm, the cost and the salt from the user's stored value
Recompute from the typed password with those, and compare in constant time
Notice that the stored cost is below the policy's
Hash the same typed password again at the policy's cost, with a fresh salt
Replace the user's stored value with the new hash
trap: Making the new hash before the old one has been verified would store whatever was typed, right or wrong, as the user's password.

prompt: With pgcrypto, `encrypt(…, 'aes')` gave two patients with one CPF identical ciphertexts. The function that uses a random session key and IV for every value, so that one CPF gives different bytes each time, is `___`.
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 14.

prompt: A monitoring check connects to the clinic's server as `www.vereda.example`, and `s_client` stops with `hostname mismatch`. The certificate covers `portal.vereda.example`. Which of these fix it as the lesson does? Choose all that apply.
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 10.

choices.text: Install the issuing CA's root certificate on the monitoring host
choices.why: That answers `unable to get local issuer certificate`; the chain was fine and the name was not.

choices.text: Point the check at `portal.vereda.example`, the name it covers
choices.why: Right: use the name the certificate covers.

choices.text: Turn off verification in the check, since the server is the clinic's own
choices.why: An impostor's certificate looks to the client exactly like this one; disabling the check accepts both.

choices.text: Issue a certificate whose SAN also carries `www.vereda.example`
choices.why: Right: a certificate covering the name the client asks for.

prompt: Offsite backups are encrypted under data keys wrapped by a KMS master key. The database server's cloud credential may call unwrap, and may also schedule that master key for deletion. What does this leave open to a ransomware attack?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 14; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 10.

choices.text: The intruder can delete that key first, and every backup goes with it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Anybody who copies the bucket can now decrypt the backups without the KMS
choices.why: The data keys are stored wrapped; reading them still takes an unwrap by an allowed identity.

choices.text: Rotating the master key now means re-encrypting every backup
choices.why: Rotation re-wraps the data keys, a few hundred bytes each, whoever holds the credential.

choices.text: The master key reaches the server in clear on every unwrap, ready to steal
choices.why: Unwrap returns a data key, briefly; the master key never leaves the KMS.

prompt: A developer keeps the system's pepper in a one-row `app_settings` table, in the same database as the Argon2id hashes, so that every application server finds it. A nightly dump of that database leaks. What has the pepper bought?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 5.

choices.text: Every guess is still blocked, since the HMAC runs before Argon2id
choices.why: The HMAC blocks guesses only for somebody who lacks its key, and this dump carries the key.

choices.text: The hashes can no longer be tied to accounts, so the leak is harmless
choices.why: The dump keeps each user beside their hash; a pepper changes the value, not whose it is.

choices.text: Each user must now reset, as the leaked pepper voids all their hashes
choices.why: The stored hashes still verify; the problem is that guessing against them is open again.

choices.text: Nothing, because the dump carries the pepper beside the hashes
choices.why: Right: a pepper is only worth something where the store is not.

prompt: Your DBA portfolio project's README says the database is backed up every night. An interviewer asks how you know the backups work. Which answer is the strong one, in the sense the lesson gives to "how do you know your tests work?"
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 12; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 1.

choices.text: The backup job has exited with status 0 every night for a month
choices.why: That is a statement about the job, not about the data: a pipe ending in `gzip` exits 0 with nothing in it.

choices.text: The dump is half a megabyte, so it is not one of the twenty-byte files a broken pipe leaves
choices.why: Size is a clue, not proof: a dump of the wrong database or one schema of three is not tiny either.

choices.text: I restored last night's dump into a second database and diffed a report against the live one
choices.why: Right: like removing the index and watching the test fail, it shows the guarantee holds.

choices.text: The script starts with `set -o pipefail`, so a failure in any program in it turns the job red
choices.why: That catches a failed program; a dump that succeeds and holds the wrong thing still exits cleanly.

prompt: Your portfolio project's committed `setup.sql` ends with `ALTER ROLE app PASSWORD 'app-lab-only';` so that anybody can rebuild the database. Taking both lessons together, what is wrong with it?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 14; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 11.

choices.text: Nothing serious: the server keeps only a SCRAM verifier, not the password that was typed
choices.why: The server stores a verifier, but the file and the statement carry the password in clear text.

choices.text: The password is in the history, and a failing run writes it into the server log too
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It stops being a problem once `setup.sql` is listed in `.gitignore` in the very next commit
choices.why: Ignoring a file stops future additions; the commit that holds the password stays in the history that is pushed.

choices.text: `ALTER ROLE` cannot set a password at all, so the script fails on that line
choices.why: It can; the lesson prefers `\password` because the statement carries the password to every place a statement goes.

prompt: You find that a commit pushed last week to your public portfolio repository contains the password of `app`, the PostgreSQL role your project connects as. What do you do first?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 14; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 11.

choices.text: Give `app` a new password with `\password app`, then update the project's environment to match
choices.why: Right: revoking is the only step that makes the leaked value useless.

choices.text: Read the server log for logins as `app`, to learn whether the password was used
choices.why: Checking for use is the second step; until the password changes, it still works for whoever has it.

choices.text: Rewrite the history with `git filter-repo` and force-push, so the scanners find nothing
choices.why: Cleaning is optional and last: it cannot recall copies already cloned, forked or cached.

choices.text: Make the repository private, since only people who could read it had the password
choices.why: A week in public is enough for clones and scanners; hiding the repository revokes nothing.

prompt: For your DBA portfolio's slow-query investigation you want realistic data. A clinic you used to work for offers an export of its appointments with the patients' names removed, keeping dates of birth, addresses and diagnoses. What do the two lessons say?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 17; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 17.

choices.text: Use it in a private repository, and publish only the query plans and the timings
choices.why: Hidden or not, you would hold patients' sensitive data with no basis for it, and it is not yours to use.

choices.text: Generate invented data: this is still personal data, and diagnoses are sensitive data
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Use it: without the names it is anonymised, and anonymised data is outside the LGPD
choices.why: Dropping the name and keeping address and date of birth still identifies people, with one more step.

choices.text: Use it once the clinic agrees in writing, as the clinic decides what is done with it
choices.why: The patients gave it for their care; the clinic's signature does not make it demo data for your portfolio.

prompt: `seed.py` lends Laptop 03 nine days before the day it runs, and loanbook's loans last seven days. If you run it a year after the lesson was recorded, by how many days is that loan past its due date on the day of the run?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 17.

prompt: In loanbook's Quadlet file, one line in the `[Service]` section makes systemd bring the container back whenever it dies: `Restart=___`.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15.

prompt: The project reads its secrets from the environment and keeps `.env` out of git. So that the next person knows what to set, the repository commits a file called `___`, listing every variable with a fake value.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 14.

prompt: You are deploying a new version of your project to srv the way the lesson does. Put the steps in order.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15.

Clone it on srv and check that the commit is the one on laptop
Build the image with `sudo podman build -t loanbook .`
Copy the `.container` file to `/etc/containers/systemd/` and run `daemon-reload`
Start the service and ask for `/healthz` from the server itself

prompt: "Why did you back the project's database up with a nightly `pg_dump` and not by archiving the WAL?" Which answer follows the lesson's four steps, with a reason the backup course would accept?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 20; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 8.

choices.text: Nightly `pg_dump`, since WAL archiving is overkill for a database this small; nobody needs it below a few gigabytes
choices.why: That argues the alternative is bad, with a general claim the interviewer may run a database to disprove.

choices.text: Nightly `pg_dump`, because it was what I knew; I had not set up WAL archiving before this project
choices.why: Honest, and it stops short: the lesson asks you to add when you would choose differently.

choices.text: Nightly `pg_dump` over WAL archiving, because `pg_dump` is simpler and it is what most teams start with
choices.why: A general truth instead of the project's facts, and no condition under which the other choice wins.

choices.text: Nightly `pg_dump`, not WAL archiving: losing a day is fine for the demo. With real orders and an RPO of minutes, I'd archive
choices.why: Right: choice, alternative, a reason in the project's own terms, and what would change it.

prompt: You are on the DBA track, choosing your portfolio project. Which does the lesson say a reviewer in your field looks for? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 3.

choices.text: A short video of the project on a real device
choices.why: That is what a mobile reviewer opens, since they will rarely install the app.

choices.text: A slow query's plan before and after the fix, measured
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The pipeline file, from a commit to something running
choices.why: That is the DevOps reviewer's first stop.

choices.text: A backup, and a restore that was actually performed
choices.why: Right.

prompt: In your third week, the shop's checkout starts failing an hour after you dropped what looked like an unused index. You think your change may be the cause. What comes first?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 22.

choices.text: Put the index back on your own, and mention it once checkout works again
choices.why: Silence while you fix it alone is how a small mistake becomes an incident.

choices.text: Post the likely cause on the status page, so support has an answer to give
choices.why: A cause is never guessed in public; a wrong one has to be retracted.

choices.text: Tell the person who needs to know, now, that your change is a likely cause
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Start the write-up's timeline now, while every time is still in the logs
choices.why: The write-up comes after the incident is over, not before anybody knows.

prompt: A command you ran on the wrong server caused a twenty-minute outage, and you are asked to draft the write-up. Which line belongs under its Actions?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 22.

choices.text: Be more careful about which server each open terminal is connected to
choices.why: "Be more careful" is not an action: it changes nothing anybody can check.

choices.text: Cause: human error by the junior who ran the command
choices.why: That is a cause, not an action, and human error is never a cause on its own.

choices.text: The junior runs nothing on production until the end of the trial period
choices.why: That punishes a person; the write-up asks how the system let a reasonable action cause harm.

choices.text: The script asks for the server's name; owner Ana, by 30 October
choices.why: Right: a change, with an owner and a date.

prompt: In your second week as a junior DBA you are asked to choose a first task. The runbook for a filling disk says it was last rehearsed two years and a major version ago. Which task fits both lessons best?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20; Database Server: Installation and Maintenance, lesson 24.

choices.text: Add the background on WAL and slots to each step, so the next junior understands it
choices.why: A runbook carries the commands, not the explanation; a training text is a different document.

choices.text: Rehearse it on a copy, fix the steps that were wrong, update the date and say it is done
choices.why: Right: small, finished properly and visible.

choices.text: Follow it on production at the next real alert, and note every step that fails
choices.why: A runbook is rehearsed before it is needed, on a server that matters to nobody.

choices.text: Turn the whole page into one script, and show it to the team once it is finished
choices.why: A large first task that drags is the worst start, and some acts need a person to ask first.

prompt: In a design interview for a junior DBA role, you are asked how you would set up the database for a small online shop. What do you do first?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 14; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 8.

choices.text: Begin with the tables and their keys, as the schema is the part a DBA owns
choices.why: The answers to the clarifying questions change the design, so they come before any drawing.

choices.text: Draw a primary, two replicas and automatic failover, since a shop has to stay open
choices.why: Parts nobody asked for read as recited, and "stay open" at any cost is a wish until somebody sees the price.

choices.text: Ask how much data the shop could lose, and for how long it could be down
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: State that it needs zero loss, and name synchronous replication as the way
choices.why: That assumes the costliest answer: every commit would wait for a second server, every day.

prompt: Your CV needs one line about the backup work in your lab. Which line follows the lesson's pattern, with evidence the backup course would count?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 4; Backup, Replication and High Availability, lesson 1.

choices.text: Set up nightly lab backups, each restored on a second server and checked
choices.why: Right: what you did, what is now true, and how anybody can check it.

choices.text: Improved backup reliability by 40% using pgBackRest, compression and retention
choices.why: A number with no baseline and no way to measure it costs more than no number.

choices.text: Was responsible for the PostgreSQL backups in a lab, using pg_dump and pgBackRest
choices.why: It opens with a phrase that hides what you did, and then lists tools.

choices.text: Helped build a backup system with pgBackRest, cron and PostgreSQL 16
choices.why: "Helped" hides your part, and the rest of the line is a list of tools.

prompt: A take-home for a junior DBA role hands you a virtual machine whose PostgreSQL will not start, with about three hours suggested. You fix it in two. Besides the working machine, what does the lesson say to hand in?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 13.

choices.text: A recording of the whole terminal session, so the reviewer sees every command
choices.why: The reviewer has about ten minutes; two hundred commands do not say which ones mattered.

choices.text: The steps, in order, that somebody else could follow, and what you checked

hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 21.
